prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints amplify and propagate economic shocks, creating the theory of credit cycles

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B006 with Kiyotaki and Moore only. I re-tested it against the round-1 exchange and the chair's questions, and I did not weigh the count of B027 supporters as evidence of merit. The case rests on four points. First, a single mechanism: borrowing limits tied to the market value of collateral create a feedback loop between asset prices and credit, so temporary shocks become large, persistent and propagated across sectors. Second, the credit is as clean as any on the shortlist, since the 1997 paper is the origin and its two authors are its originators. Several members who rank B027 first say the same, including Andersson, Boppart, Fredriksson, Krusell and Hjalmarsson. Third, maturity is not in question after almost thirty years of extension and application. Fourth, the 2007-09 crisis made the mechanism's relevance concrete. Teorell asked how I would separate this from the 2022 prize in a citation. The 2022 prize rewarded the analysis of banks, bank runs and the history of banking crises. Kiyotaki-Moore is a dynamic general-equilibrium mechanism that runs through asset prices and the borrowing capacity of productive agents, and it does not depend on a banking sector. The citation therefore names collateral constraints and credit cycles and says nothing about banks or runs. I keep Gertler and Gilchrist out because the accelerator lineage is the part closest to what was recognised in 2022. Stromberg is right that the committee should state this reasoning, not treat the omission as obvious, and I would put it on the record. On the chair's question about the weaker direct identification, I do not regard it as disqualifying. The size of the amplification is inferred through calibrated models and later empirical work, not through a single design, and that is why I rank B006 where I do, as a judgment about confirmation and not about importance.
statement.case_against: Three reservations remain. The first is partial redundancy with the 2022 prize and the Bernanke-Gertler lineage. A committee that reads the macro-finance theme as already recognised would reasonably not choose B006 this year. The second is that the contribution is mainly theoretical and its quantitative importance is established indirectly, whereas B027 rests on evidence that has been examined and contested in many settings. The third is that I am the chair, a macroeconomist, and a minority of two on B006. I may overweight a clean theoretical mechanism relative to broad empirical confirmation. Several colleagues who rank B027 first (Hjalmarsson, Fredriksson, Boppart) weigh that tradeoff differently, and their reasons are scientific and not tactical. B027 also has a coherent citation available. The question is the one the chair raised, whether to write it around labour demand, wages and local labour markets or around the import-competition work alone. The Katz-versus-Dorn cost is real, but several supporters have shown the citation can be worded to manage the Acemoglu and Goldin overlap.

responses.point: Stromberg also prefers Kiyotaki and Moore alone. He argues the mechanism is distinct from the bank-centred 2022 work because it is dynamic and runs through asset prices. He also says the committee should explain why Gertler is omitted and not treat the omission as obvious.
responses.response: I agree with the distinctness argument and have used it above as the basis for the citation wording. I accept your point on Gertler. The omission should rest on a stated reason, namely that the accelerator strand overlaps most with 2022 and that his later intermediation work is better weighed elsewhere, and not on a default. I am more cautious than you about the strength of the case. You describe B027 as a close second, and I think the disagreement between us and the B027 camp is about how much empirical confirmation should count against a clean originator pair. I would not call it a disagreement about scientific standing.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B027 first and said he would like to hear how I separate Kiyotaki-Moore from the 2022 work in a citation. He also said he would support Autor, Dorn and Hanson over his own trio if the citation were narrowed to trade exposure.
responses.response: I have tried to answer your question directly above: the citation concerns collateral values and credit cycles, and the 2022 prize concerned banks and runs. Your concession on the third name confirms my main reservation about B027. If the technology-and-trade citation is adopted, the committee must accept either Dorn's exclusion or a narrower prize, and your own file says the two trios imply different citations. That cost is real, but it does not decide the question for me. I now regard a coherent B027 citation as available, which is a change from my round-1 position that I could not resolve it. I still place B006 first because its attribution needs no such trade-off.

responses.point: Krusell now names Autor, Hanson and Katz for B027. In round 1 he accepted the two-name Kiyotaki-Moore core as cleaner than his earlier three-name proposal, while placing B006 behind B027 because the mechanism is foundational but mostly theoretical with a real question about marginal novelty after 2022.
responses.response: I accept your account of why you moved, and I am glad we agree on two names for B006. On marginal novelty, the 2022 prize and Kiyotaki-Moore address different objects, so I do not think the redundancy question is as severe as you suggest, but I take it seriously enough to keep it as my main uncertainty. I also note that you and Teorell are the colleagues most concerned about whether B027 is one achievement or two. That concern affects the strength of B027's citation as much as the thinner identification affects B006's.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B006 second. She says the 2022 overlap is non-trivial and the committee would have to explain what is new, but she would back B006 if attribution proved fatal for B027. She also says first-place counts do not measure scientific merit.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The committee would have to explain what is new relative to 2022, and I have tried to do that above. I also agree that counts do not measure merit, and that applies equally to my own minority position. Your conditional support is useful because it shows B006 and B027 are not rival views of what matters. The question is which attribution problem the committee can live with. I would put it that way when members vote.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B027 first and says the Goldin and Acemoglu work address different questions from the distributional effects of tasks and trade shocks, so the 2023 and 2024 overlap is smaller than I implied. She regards B006 as having very clean attribution but thinner empirical confirmation.
responses.response: That is a fair correction. My round-1 reference to the Acemoglu and Goldin prizes was about the three-name cap and the task framework's wider authorship, and I accept that the overlap is probably smaller than I suggested. I would take the overlap off the list of reasons I hold back from B027. What remains is the Katz-versus-Dorn cost and the one-or-two-achievements question, which your own file lists as the main reservation. I agree that replication scrutiny is the strongest argument for B027, and it is why B027 remains my first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads Kiyotaki-Moore as sufficiently distinct from the 2022 prize and the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator lineage, and whether my citation wording is enough to make that clear.
Whether Gertler, and possibly Gilchrist, should be added on the merits of their intermediation work, and how that interacts with Gertler's appearance in B018.
How much a clean originator attribution should count against the broader and more directly tested empirical evidence behind B027. I am not sure my weighting is right.
Whether B027 can carry one coherent citation without a contestable choice between Katz and Dorn. I now regard it as possible but costly.
My assessments rely on my own knowledge of the literature and the supplied files. I have not independently verified any source, and the nine-name B027 support count is not evidence of merit.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the credited names of B006, B027 or B012 is apparent from my profile. I disclose my committee ties without adjudicating them. I have co-authored with committee members Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg, including a 2026 IJIO paper with Friberg and Tore Ellingsen, and frequently with Per Krusell, the secretary. Krusell and Boppart are IIES colleagues, and Teorell is also at Stockholm University. The 2018 Scientific Background cites my own work, and whether I drafted any of it is not documented. I am a macroeconomist, which may bias me toward macro candidates, and I wrote the round-1 chair summary, so I have tried to treat it only as a record of the round-1 files and not as evidence for or against any candidate. Friberg's marriage to a former Swedish prime minister is public and has no apparent bearing on any shortlisted candidate. No recusal is assumed.
